explanations.explanation: The text says it plainly: "All your rulers have fled together, captured without a bow." So the people in charge ran, and they ran as a group. I think that's the group project nobody wanted to be in charge of.

I get the pull of this one, friend, because praying sounds like a fine thing for rulers to do. But the verse doesn't say they prayed. It says "All your rulers have fled together, captured without a bow." Running is what the text gives us.
Staying put is the exact opposite of what the verse says. "All your rulers have fled together…" it tells us. They left, and the verse says they were captured without a bow.

The rulers were "…captured without a bow." and the fugitives "…were captured together, having fled to a distant place." Think about that. They fled, even to a distant place, and still ended up captured. So the running ended in captivity.

That's what running is supposed to do, and I see why you went there. But verse 3 says the rulers were captured, and the fugitives were captured together too. They fled to a distant place and still got caught. Safety never shows up in the verse.

Battle sounds close, but look at verse 2. The slain "…did not die by the sword, nor were they killed in battle." Verse 3 says the rulers were captured without a bow, and the fugitives were captured too. So the verse lands on captivity.

It's an easy thing to assume, since most of us want company when we're sad. But the prophet says the opposite: "Turn away from me, let me weep bitterly! Do not try to console me over the destruction of the daughter of my people." He wants room to weep. I think this grief runs deep.

Right, baker. The prophet says, "Turn away from me, let me weep bitterly! Do not try to console me over the destruction of the daughter of my people." He asks people to turn away and not console him. I think this is a heavy moment, so let it be heavy.

Verse 5 says it straight: "…the Lord GOD of Hosts has set a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the Valley of Vision…" The day belongs to Him. That's why the prophet's weeping carries so much weight.
The rulers don't set anything here, friend. Back in verse 3 they're the ones who fled and got captured. The day comes from "…the Lord GOD of Hosts…" as verse 5 says.

Priests never come up in these verses. The text names who set the day: "…the Lord GOD of Hosts has set a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the Valley of Vision…" Sometimes the answer is just sitting in the verse, waiting for us to read it.

Verse 7 says, "Your choicest valleys are full of chariots, and horsemen are posted at the gates." So the best land is packed with chariots, and the gates have horsemen posted there. A gate is the front door of a city, and I'd say that door has company.
Water does come up in this passage, but later. In verse 9 the people collect water from the lower pool. Verse 7 puts the horsemen at the gates.
Altars never show up in these verses, baker. The text says, "…horsemen are posted at the gates." That's where the horsemen stand, right at the city's entrance.

explanations.answer: The weapons in the House of the Forest
explanations.explanation: Verse 8 says, "On that day you looked to the weapons in the House of the Forest." When the defenses were uncovered, that's where their eyes went. Remember it, because verse 11 comes back to where they did and didn't look.

explanations.answer: The gold stored in the temple treasury
explanations.explanation: Gold sounds like a fair thing to grab in a crisis, but the verse doesn't mention it. It says the people looked to "…the weapons in the House of the Forest." Weapons are what they turned to.

explanations.answer: The horses sent up from Egypt
explanations.explanation: Horses do show up in this passage, but they belong to the invaders in verses 6 and 7. Nothing in these verses sends horses up from Egypt. In verse 8, the people looked to "…the weapons in the House of the Forest."

explanations.answer: To tear them down for the wall
explanations.explanation: Verse 10 says, "You counted the houses of Jerusalem and tore them down to strengthen the wall." They tore houses down to strengthen the wall. Imagine counting your own street just to see how much of it you can pull down.

explanations.answer: To find room for the soldiers
explanations.explanation: The verse gives a different reason, friend. It says they "…tore them down to strengthen the wall." Housing for soldiers isn't in the text.

explanations.answer: To collect a tax for weapons
explanations.explanation: Taxes never come up here. Verse 10 says, "You counted the houses of Jerusalem and tore them down to strengthen the wall." The count came first, then the tearing down.

explanations.answer: Looking to the One who made it
explanations.explanation: Verse 11 says, "…you did not look to the One who made it, or consider Him who planned it long ago." They built a reservoir for the ancient pool's waters, but they didn't look to Him. That's the part that was missing, so don't skip it.

explanations.answer: Enough workers to finish the job
explanations.explanation: The text says they built it, so the work got done. Nothing says they ran short of workers. The missing piece is in verse 11: "…you did not look to the One who made it, or consider Him who planned it long ago."

explanations.answer: Enough stone to repair the wall
explanations.explanation: No stone shortage is mentioned in these verses, baker. They built a reservoir between the walls, and they tore down houses to strengthen the wall. What the prophet says was missing is in verse 11: "…you did not look to the One who made it…"

Verse 12 says, "On that day the Lord GOD of Hosts called for weeping and wailing, for shaven heads and the wearing of sackcloth." That's a call to grieve. It's a sober call, and the next verse shows what the people did with it.

Feasting is what the people did, not what God called for. Verse 12 says He "…called for weeping and wailing, for shaven heads and the wearing of sackcloth." Verse 13 is where the meat and wine show up.
No singing here, friend. Verse 12 says the Lord GOD of Hosts "…called for weeping and wailing…" Shaven heads and sackcloth came with it.

Verse 13 says it: "…there is joy and gladness, butchering of cattle and slaughtering of sheep, eating of meat and drinking of wine…" Their words were, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!" Verse 12 had called for weeping, so the feast went the other way.

The text says otherwise. Verse 13 reads, "…there is joy and gladness, butchering of cattle and slaughtering of sheep, eating of meat and drinking of wine…" Right after the call to weep in verse 12, the people feast and say, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!"
The LORD of Hosts says, "Until your dying day, this sin of yours will never be atoned for…" That's a serious word, and it comes right after the feast. I'd just let it sit for a moment, baker.
That's a hopeful word, and I see why it tempted you. But the LORD of Hosts says, "Until your dying day, this sin of yours will never be atoned for…" The verse says never.
"Surely" sounds strong, and this verse is strong. But the word in the verse is "never." The LORD of Hosts says, "Until your dying day, this sin of yours will never be atoned for…"
